Adds Memro's MCP server and recalls the project's memory at the start of every session. See integrations/claude-code . title: Show HN: Comemo – composite memory provider for Hermes Agent
summary: There are many memory providers that can be used externally with Hermes Agent. However, like many other AI agents, Hermes only provides one slot for an external memory provider. Comemo takes that slot and acts as a composite provider. How? It fans out memory writes to multiple backends such as Mem0, Honcho, and Supermemory. On retrieval, it queries the enabled providers, merges their results, and removes duplicates before returning them to Hermes. I intend to add support for more memory providers and eventually extend Comemo to other open-source AI agents with similar limitations.
story_key: story|title:comemo composite memory provider for hermes agent
content_excerpt: Composite memory meta-provider for Hermes Agent. Use Honcho, Mem0, and Supermemory simultaneously. Comemo is a composite memory provider for Hermes Agent. It runs multiple memory providers at the same time instead of one. Hermes lets you pick one memory provider. You can use Honcho, Mem0, Supermemory, or Hindsight, but only one at a time. Comemo sits in that single slot and writes to all of them at once. Reads come back merged and deduplicated. If one provider fails, the others keep running. Hermes only activates one at a time. This is a known constraint ( Issue #24770 , marked wontfix in core). The maintainers asked the community to build a composite provider as a catalog plugin instead. On every write, Comemo fans out to all active providers in parallel using a thread pool. If a provider fails, the write goes into a local SQLite retry queue and replays at the next session start. On every read, Comemo queries all active providers in parallel, merges the results, and deduplicates identical lines before returning to Hermes. Then run hermes memory setup — Hermes walks through enabling each provider and stores API keys securely in its secret scope. Restart Hermes after and Comemo is live. After install: run hermes memory setup — Hermes presents each field from the config schema, writes non-secret settings to ~/.hermes/config.yaml , and stores API keys securely in its secret scope. Runs the setup wizard. Prompts for which providers to enable and writes non-secret settings to ~/.hermes/config.yaml . Run hermes memory setup separately to set API keys. Connects to each enabled provider and does a real write and read. Confirms the providers are reachable and working, not just configured. Queries all enabled providers and shows what is stored. Uses a broad recall by default so you get recent memories without needing to know what to search for. Use --query to filter by topic and --limit to control how many entries are shown per provider (default 20): Cloud memory that understands who you are over time, not just what was said. Tracks identity and context across sessions using a workspace-scoped store. Reads every conversation and automatically extracts facts like preferences, context, and recurring topics. Retrieves the most relevant ones at the start of each turn. Structured knowledge storage with 3-layer retrieval: user profile, entity graph, and document RAG. Memories are scoped to a namespace. title: Artex: Open-source AI Pentest Framework that is bacoming hackers favorite tool
story_key: story|title:artex open source ai pentest framework that is bacoming hackers favorite tool
content_excerpt: ARTEX went from a July GitHub release to bank breaches, a ConnectWise supply-chain compromise and a 200-target espionage campaign. What its agents do, what they leave in logs, and what to close first. ARTEX matters because it automated the expensive part of penetration testing: chaining ordinary weaknesses at machine speed. Within three months of its July 2026 GitHub release it was used against South Korean banks, in a supply-chain compromise and in a 200-target espionage campaign. Wiz Research reports that a Chinese developer published it, that it won Baidu's "Agent+" red-team challenge that September, and that the project went closed-source on October 8, after attackers had already used it against South Korean banks ( Wiz Research, October 22, 2026 ). That is a short runway for a security tool. By November, Microsoft had published two reports on actors using it, CrowdStrike had published two more, Seoul police had described a criminal case built on it, and independent scanners were counting exposed consoles by the thousand. The tool did not create a new class of vulnerability. It changed how quickly ordinary weaknesses can be tried, retried and chained. The important shift is economic. A human pentester is limited by hours, attention and skill. An agent fleet is limited by tokens, proxies and targets. Microsoft's assessment of one campaign found several cases where the time from initial targeting to privileged cloud access was under three hours ( Microsoft, October 21, 2026 ). Unit 42 describes operators turning public password-reset pages and exposed APIs into cloud access "sometimes in less than a day" without exploiting a single software vulnerability ( Unit 42, November 11, 2026 ). ARTEX is an orchestration system for agents, tools and evidence, not a scanner with an LLM bolted on. A public fork of the project publishes a README that describes a Go monolith that embeds a Next.js frontend, a PostgreSQL database, and an agent runtime built on the author's norma SDK ( ARTEX README , a public fork of the upstream project). Four roles share the work: a Goals agent decomposes the target and extracts scope, a Planner produces the next intent, Worker agents execute tools, and a MainAgent keeps a human in the loop. Two graphs hold the state. The asset graph is global and shared across tasks: root domains, subdomains, IPs, services, apps and endpoints, grouped by company. The exploration graph is per task: goals, intents, facts, findings and hints, linked by e

title: Can KV Cache Be Reused Across Model Updates? A DeepSeek-V4-Flash Case Study
summary: Reusing key--value (KV) caches across language model updates could avoid repeated computation of shared context, but changes in model weights raise a fundamental question about what these caches preserve. We investigate direct cache reuse across four model updates, with a detailed study of DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Flash-0731. Our central finding is that caches can retain useful task information without faithfully reproducing the updated model's behavior. Retrieval accuracy varies substantially across updates, ranging from near-native performance to large losses. With source caches already available, reuse achieves median time-to-first-token speedups of $2.10$--$5.08\times$ on three longer-prefix QA benchmarks. To characterize the behavioral differences behind these outcomes, we introduce Functional Cache Divergence, which compares next-token distributions under reused and native caches. Direct KV cache reuse better preserves native model behavior in natural-text continuation, whereas compatibility degrades with increasing prefix length in single-token retrieval tasks. Answer-margin analyses help explain how correct retrieval decisions survive substantial internal state changes. Yet even agreement on the first generated token does not ensure agreement in answer content or stopping behavior. These findings establish task utility and fidelity to native inference as distinct criteria for evaluating cross-version KV cache reuse.

title: Evaluating Feedback-Driven Black-Box Processes via Stochastic Modeling and Simulation
summary: We study feedback-driven black-box processes across software engineering and machine learning. These processes are inherently sequential: policies generate inputs, observe outputs/feedback from systems, and use the feedback to guide the design of subsequent inputs. While many policies are developed under structural assumptions on the underlying systems, many real-world systems operate without such knowledge, necessitating black-box policies that lack a unified evaluation framework. We introduce a stochastic framework that models and evaluates such policies using Markov chains and simulation, thereby connecting empirical practice with theory. We instantiate the framework in mutation-based fuzzing (widely used for discovering software bugs via sequential input mutation), by a novel Markov chain model of fuzzing whose transitions are governed by the mutation strategy and whose feedback is given by program execution. We develop a rigorous evaluation paradigm with new performance measures, sound estimators, and evaluation procedures with provable guarantees. Guided by the theory, we evaluate 9 fuzzers on 18 widely used fuzzing benchmarks and conduct case studies in 4 non-fuzzing domains. These results show that the framework provides a principled basis for evaluation while connecting to practice, with implications beyond fuzzing.

title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.

summary: See how Workday used LangGraph and LangSmith to build an internal AI agent platform that cut prototype time from months to less than a day and compliance needs.
story_key: model:langgraph|title:how workday built an enterprise scale ai agent platform with langgraph and langs
content_excerpt: Workday is the trusted agentic platform for HR, finance, and IT, serving more than half the Fortune 500. The team set out to create the internal developer platform to build, deploy, and run AI agents in production, on Workday's infrastructure. The team leveraged LangGraph for agent orchestration and LangSmith for tracing, observability, and evals. In 2025, Workday’s leadership team saw the market opportunity for building agentic solutions and set an ambitious goal for agents in production by the end of 2026. Product teams needed a platform that could support both rapid prototyping and production deployments—a uniquely challenging mandate given Workday operates under some of the strictest security and data governance requirements in enterprise software. Getting any internal service into production means satisfying demanding audit, compliance, and data retention policies. The surface area was enormous for a team of four, encompassing a durable, scalable agent server; data access controls tied to Workday's audit policies; a collaborative eval platform; and an SDK that abstracted all of it. Workday’s Agent Platform team serves two user bases. 1.) the internal Workday engineering teams building agents, and 2.) the end customers of those agents. It lets teams focus on functional requirements, while handling authentication, security, compliance, and infrastructure. The first major product shipped was Workday's Agent System of Record, a governance layer that controls which APIs the agents are allowed to access. The Agent Platform team built the backend server and eval infrastructure that the system of record runs on top of. The team also built what Alex Gatto, Senior Machine Learning Engineer, describes as "Workday LangChain": a Python SDK that wraps LangChain primitives and routes them through Workday's internal services, including an LLM gateway, a RAG retrieval service, and other internal tooling. "Anytime there was some AI concept that LangChain had put out, we tried to build a Python SDK for that same concept, but at Workday," explained Alex. Workday chose LangGraph for agent orchestration to give internal developers maximum flexibility at the design layer, while providing standardized infrastructure underneath.
